=== FILE: Can You Eat Pizza And Still Lose Weight？ ＊Spoiler＊ YES! [UO1mdMl3Xb4].txt ===

 you can eat pizza and still lose weight. One of the things I kind of made popular was flexible dieting, meaning you can eat whatever food you want as long as it fits into your macronutrient goals for the day. You can eat whatever you want and still lose weight in terms of the food choices, but you can't eat however much you want of the food that you want. And when it comes to something like pizza, which is very calorie dense, I have a high energy expenditure, pretty high lean body mass, I can diet on like 27, 2800 calories a day and lose body fat. I got rumored there that if I want to have, you know, 6, 700 calories from a few slices of pizza, I can and I can still hit my fiber targets, I can still hit my protein targets. But if you're a smaller woman with less lean mass, you're not that active and you need to have, you know, 14, 13, 1400 calories to lose weight, do you want to chew up half of that on a couple slices of pizza? Giving people the option to have those foods actually can help increase adherence for a lot of people because they don't feel so deprived, but you got to be smart about it. If you are somebody who just can't diet on a lot of calories, you're probably going to have to make a lot of quote unquote clean food choices, minimally processed foods, whole foods for satiety, because otherwise you're going to be really, really hungry. But again, if you're somebody like me, quite a bit of lean mass, a lot of energy expenditure, if you want to have a little bit of junk food or processed food, if you can still hit your other requirements, it's fine. It's kind of like a budget. If I make a million bucks a year and I want to buy $100,000 sports car, but I can do that and still take care of my responsibilities and that $100,000 sports car makes me feel good and like gives me a little bit of like, you know, it's like a car on the end of the stick motivates me a little bit, then yeah, that's fine. But it might be a good investment because it makes me feel good about the work I've been doing. Alternatively, if you make 50 grand a year, is it a good idea to go out and buy a brand new sports car? Probably not. If it means that you can't pay your mortgage, you can't save for retirement, you can't cover your health insurance. So nutrition is kind of the same way. If you can still hit your obligations on a day-to-day basis, protein, fiber, calories, then yeah, it's okay to have some junk or depreciating asset as part of it. But if it's that junk is going to put you over your macros or you're not going to get enough protein or fiber in, then no, it's not a good idea. That's why Carbon Diet Coach is so useful because you can see what you're consuming. You can come up with a dietary budget and we allow maximum flexibility because you can do balanced diet, you can do low fat, low carb, ketogenic, plant-based, and you can do intermittent fasting or regular meal feeding. You can have two meals per day. You can have seven meals per day. We allow for maximum flexibility so that you can have the best adherence possible because that is what matters. If you guys are interested in my app, you can download and subscribe with the link in my bio.

こfaloobili, your leptin increases, your insulin increases, and some other hormones can be affected. As you lose body fat, your leptin decreases, your insulin decreases. === FILE: NSAIDs Are Killing Muscle？ [atHo6ncVizc].en.txt ===

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, incaids like ibuprofen may actually inhibit muscle hypertrophy and muscle protein synthesis. When you resistance train and you place mechanical tension on a muscle, part of the process that's involved in muscle tissue remodeling involves inflammatory cytoine and inhibiting these inflammatory cytoines may actually inhibit muscle growth. So in young people when they give high doses of insaids, it does attenuate hypertrophy. It reduces the hypertrophy response to resistance training. What's interesting though is in elderly people the opposite thing happened. There was either no effect of insaids or there was a slight benefit to incaids on muscle hypertrophy. But I think what's likely is that there is kind of this U shape or inverted U shape for hypertrophy and inflammation where you have an optimal range of inflammation and too little inflammation is not conducive for hypertrophy and too much inflammation is not conducive for hypertrophy. >> [music]

=== FILE: Never Feel Hungry on a Diet Again： 5 Fullness Hacks That Actually Work [YXuHmRKFcxo].txt ===

 five ways to stay full on a fat loss diet. Going through fat loss, being in the calorie deficit, you're probably gonna feel hungry at various points, but there are things you can do to improve your satiety. Tip one, eat high fiber. Fiber has been shown to be filling, improve satiety. In the case of things like insoluble fiber, insoluble fibers like cellulose and hemicellulose, they pull water into your GI tract. This increases sensation of fullness and can increase not just your GI sensation of fullness, but tell your brain that you actually are more full. Tip two, eat a high protein diet. Protein not only increases energy expenditure, but it's also been shown to improve satiety. And this effect is consistent even across minimally processed foods and highly processed foods. So no matter what your diet consists of, eating more protein is gonna be beneficial for your appetite regulation. Tip three, eat slowly and mindfully. So chew many, many bites, kind of as many as you can, and eat slow purposefully and focus on what you're doing. There's research studies to show that if you mindfully eat and you eat slowly, then you actually eat less overall. So your eating rate matters. Tip four, drink fluid. There is research showing that if you do preloads before a meal with water or any kind of fluid, except for obviously sugar, sweetened beverages, that that can induce sensations of fullness and help you in the meal faster. So if you drink some water, make sure you're hydrated or drink even a diet soda or something like that, that can help with sensation of fullness and help you feel like you don't wanna eat as much. Tip five, eat mostly whole food minimally processed. Now this goes along with eating a high fiber diet. High fiber diets are hard to do if you're eating a lot of processed food because most processed foods don't have a lot of fiber in them. So they kind of go hand in hand. But research has shown that switching from a minimally processed diet to an ultra processed diet can spontaneously increase caloric intake by over 500 calories overnight. So if you want to have better appetite regulation, choose minimally processed whole foods. They're more filling, they have more fiber and they're gonna have a better effect on your overall appetite. Now if you guys don't know where to get started with nutrition, check out my app, Carbon Diet Coach. Carbon takes all the guesswork out of it. How many calories you should eat for your goal, for your individual metabolism, and what your macronutrient composition should be, and it adjusts to your dietary preferences and your lifestyle. It is a phenomenal tool, I can't recommend it enough. Check out the link in my bio and go follow them at Carbon Diet Coach.

=== FILE: No One Talks About This Side of Weight Loss [7VZEpti0VRE].txt ===

 Have you lost a significant amount of body weight, but you still feel like you're fat, like you're in your head all the time, you always see yourself as the before, you're not seen after? This is a common thing that many people go through, and unfortunately, while losing weight can help with body image, it doesn't always fix the root problem. And many people who lose weight actually sometimes get even worse body image issues. And so, if you're not trying to correct for the core problem of never feeling good enough, there's no amount of weight loss you're going to be able to do that's going to make you feel like you hit a goal. I have worked with some of the highest level physique competitors in the world, by all objective measurements, people with the best bodies on the planet. And I can tell you that many of them felt like they were too fat. Many of them were afraid to go out in public at various times. Many of them canceled events, dinners, public things, because they felt they were too fat, even though they were leaner than 99.9% of people on the planet. So, unfortunately, if you don't address the root causes of body dysmorphia, no matter how much weight you lose, no matter how lean you get, no matter how much muscle you build, those issues will persist. So, if you are somebody who's struggling with body image issues, I would highly recommend working with a therapist who works with cognitive behavioral therapy, because that has been shown to help improve some of these body image issues. And some body image issues also can lead to more sinister things like eating disorders, anorexia, bulinia. It can be a pretty serious issue, especially when you consider that eating disorders, not depression, are actually the leading cause of mortality in mental health disorders. They have the highest mortality rate of all mental health disorders. People may be surprised to learn that. And they don't talk about it very much, and a lot of it stems from never feeling good enough. If you're somebody who's struggling with this, I highly recommend getting help. If you just will lose a few pounds, it's fine. I'm not saying don't lose weight, because you're never going to feel better about yourself. You may very well feel better about yourself. I think what I'm trying to say is short of having some sort of psychological issue, make sure you're celebrating your wins. Make sure if you lose five pounds, and you're not to your goal, you still feel like you don't look the way you want. Still give yourself credit for losing the five pounds that you did lose, because if you don't do that, it's going to be really hard to stick it out when things get tough.

=== FILE: Ozempic, Wegovy & GLP-1s： What They Don’t Teach You About Keeping the Weight Off [Abow2BezUuc].txt ===

 what GLP-1s don't teach you. GLP-1s are a great tool, but you can't just use them alone. If you want to get the best results possible, you need to still focus on building healthy habits. Now, GLP-1s can be a great springboard to help build healthy habits because they are powerful appetite suppressants, but there's still work you've got to do as well. When it comes to GLP-1s, by all metrics, they are the most effective weight loss tools that we've ever seen. In research studies, you see up to like 20% of body weight loss on average with things like trisepotide, which is a GLP-1-GIP memetic combo. And not only that, we're seeing evidence that GLP-1 memetics may even help with just like addictive and impulsive behaviors overall. But we also have to look at practically what that can do in terms of appetite suppression. My friend, Peter Atia, talks about this, where he notices people who take GLP-1s, they tend to eat less protein overall, because if you don't have a big appetite, protein a lot of times is the last thing you want to eat. Or you don't want to eat really fibrous foods because you don't have a big appetite. And so if you're somebody who goes from eating kind of a crappy diet overall to eating just less of a crappy diet, you will lose weight because you're consuming less calories, but you're not going to be getting enough fiber. You're not going to be getting enough protein. And the loss of the weight, the composition of it, is going to be more skewed towards losing more lean mass versus losing fat mass. And so my advice is still similar to people who are undergoing weight loss without GLP-1s. You want to focus on getting enough protein and getting enough fiber. And especially when you don't have a big appetite and you're not hungry, this is where using tracking tools and coaching tools like Carbon Diet Coach can really come in handy because many people just don't know what they're consuming. And I promise you, if I take somebody and have them track everything in carbon, a lot of times after a few days they go, oh my God, I'm only eating like nine grams of fiber a day. Or oh my gosh, I was only eating like 50 grams of protein a day. And that's where carbon really shines. Because as we've talked about many times, yes, the total calories you consume, that is the most important metric for losing weight. And GLP-1s can absolutely help with that. But the next two most important metrics are making sure you get enough protein in to support your lean mass because you do not want to lose a bunch of lean mass. There are very, very negative health outcomes and longevity outcomes and quality of life outcomes from losing lean mass. And oh by the way, it also increases your risk of regaining body fat if you lose more lean mass. And then the second thing is getting enough dietary fiber because dietary fiber has a myriad of health benefits and is good for longevity. And literally every single study looking at dietary fiber intake and the risk of mortality from a bunch of different causes, they find that dietary fiber intake reduces that risk. And it is a very consistent effect. So I don't want you to just lose weight but still not really get that much healthier. So you need to focus on making sure you keep your protein and your fiber up even when you're on GLP ones. And carbon can be a great tool to help with that. And that's really the goal with reverse dieting is slowly increasing your calories, uh, from your current estimated maintenance, uh, to bring your metabolic rate up. So it kind of pushes the metabolic rate up and up and up and up, uh, as far as it can go. Um, and it does that because in the same way, it's like the opposite of dieting, you know, as you're dieting, your metabolism is slowing down, uh, and being more, it's conserving, you know, energy more, but as you eat more food, your body gets more wasteful with the calories and you burn more calories. Uh, and so, uh, it's the opposite and you, you want to push your maintenance calories up as high as you can post diet, just so you are set up for more long-term success. Um, and it's, it's different like with, so with carbon, we have a reverse diet setting and we also have like a weight gain setting. They're both putting you in a surplus. Weight gain tends to be more of a surplus, um, with reverse diet. It's a very slight surplus from your estimated maintenance. And, um, there might be confusion there with some people thinking, um, after a diet, it slowly brings your calories up from deficit to maintenance, but we instantly bring your calories up to estimated maintenance, which by definition will not cause you to gain body fat or anything like that. You might see some water, um, water fluctuation, but it'll bring you to your estimated maintenance, which is lower than your pre diet maintenance. And at that point, then it's going to slowly try to push your, um, metabolic rate up and up by giving you small calorie increases each week, as long as you aren't gaining too much weight. So it's slightly different than the weight gain in that, um, it's going to increase your calories as long as you aren't gaining too much weight. Whereas with weight gain, it's going to make sure it's going to force your body to gain a certain amount of weight each week. So hopefully that makes sense. Because if they were really in the 400 calorie increase in energy expenditure per day, you would see differences in body weight over time. They did not report body weight. I need some help, please. The first week of my fat loss journey, I dropped six pounds and I got an increase of 300 calories. I'm aware a large share of this is water weight. Now I'm halfway through week three and I haven't lost anything. I've gone up a pound or two, then returned, but nothing else. Do I need to stick with the fat loss or do I need to switch to maintenance? Any experiences with staying on, staying out at a weight for a couple of weeks, then a big drop. Thank you. So weight loss is not linear. You will notice that, you know, at the beginning of a diet, you're going to typically drop weight faster and then it'll slow down towards the end. What carbon does is if you take a step back and look at your overall progress on the fat loss or the weight loss goal, for example, what it tries to do is keep your average progress right in line with what you have set. So you may lose a bunch at the beginning, for example, that six pounds in your first week. And then you say you haven't lost any in week two and three. Well, you're still on track with what you said you wanted to lose on average per week. The important thing is being consistent and sticking with it. I know you like seeing the big drop at the beginning and you want to keep getting a lot of progress, but it's good to dial it back and go more with what the average you have set is. So I would just be patient. The worst thing you can do, in my opinion, is switch goals. I would stick it out. It's only your third week. Your progress is going to pick back up and carbon is going to adjust your macros so that you're progressing as close as possible to what you set for your goal. So just be patient, stick it out, and it should adjust and get you dialed, dialing you in right where you need to be. So thanks for the question, Zachary. It looks like we're getting a few on IG here. I'll pull those up. Love to know your thoughts on the carnivore diet. Honestly, I haven't thought much about the carnivore diet. It just seems like a very extreme dieting approach. I, as a registered dietitian, you know, I understand the importance of fruits and vegetables and getting, you know, plenty of fiber in your diet as well for, for your health. And so I don't believe the carnivore diet is going to be something that people should do just because you, you aren't getting your fruits and vegetables and those are important as well. So I wouldn't recommend a strict diet like the carnivore diet. We preach balance at carbon. So, you know, balance in all things, we don't take any extreme approaches in terms of dieting. So I wouldn't recommend the carnivore diet, but I honestly, I haven't even dug too much into it just because it's not anything that I would ever do. Thanks for the question. Is it normal to have GI upset when increasing protein intake? Yeah, absolutely. It's, if your body's not used to a higher protein diet, it is going to take probably a few weeks before you, you, your body adapts and your GI adapts to the higher protein intake. Now, if it's like really excessive amount of protein, you might, you might always kind of have GI upset from going super, super high in protein. So I would make sure you're eating a moderate amount of protein and a good amount for whatever your goals are. And if you're using carbon, it'll set your protein in an optimal ratio. And it'll even provide a slider to where you can adjust within. So it'll have a minimum amount that we recommend for you based on your goal, and then a maximum amount. And I would just experiment within that range until you don't really get any GI discomfort anymore. If I'm skinny fat, should I focus on losing fat or gaining muscle? Typically with skinny fat, I would recommend focusing on building muscle and prioritizing that because focusing on your weight training and doing the things that you need to do to build muscle are going to also help, help improve your metabolism, which will help you be able to maintain on higher calories. And then you'll have more lean body mass and all these things are going to help get rid of the skinny fat over the longterm. So focus on building muscle. And then unless you're like really, really, really high body fat percentage and you just feel really uncomfortable, I would focus on building muscle first. And then later, once you're happy with your muscle mass, then you can do a fat loss phase to strip some of the body fat. But yeah, that's what I would do in that scenario. After going through a weight gain phase, would you recommend changing to maintenance or weight loss in that? I mean, it all depends on your goals. After a gain phase, you really can do anything. But if you're happy with where you are at and just want to maintain, then you can go to maintain weight goal. So yeah, it just depends on where you want to go. But the ending a gain phase, it's pretty much open to basically anything you want to do. Let's see. Looks like we got one on YouTube from Wayne. What is a reverse diet and when should you do it? Great question, Wayne. So reverse dieting is a strategy to help optimize your metabolism. And it's typically done at the end of like a weight loss phase. Because when you try to lose weight, you need to eat fewer calories than your body requires to lose weight and body fat. And that is going to have an impact on your metabolism. So your body adapts to everything you do in terms of how you're dieting and stuff. So when you're in a dieting phase, your body's going to slow down its metabolism to help preserve the body fat stores and the things that it has and the energy it has. And so you're going to burn fewer calories from that. You want to kind of undo that negative metabolic adaptation at the end of a diet. And that's when a reverse diet comes in. And you know, it's, it's like slow and controlled increasing calories to, to see where you kind of reach a tipping point in terms of your metabolism, where you increase calories and you put on like an excessive amount of weight. So like, you're able to slowly increase calories week to week and your metabolism speeds up to offset that. And if, if the adjustments are small enough, typically you can increase, keep increasing week to week and not see too much weight gain in comparison to what you would think you would be getting at those calories. And you'll get a point where, like I said, like a tipping point of where you've optimized your metabolism, and then you'll start seeing linear weight gain from increases in calories. And then you typically want to back out. Now reverse diet is just an approach to kind of undo those negative metabolic adaptations in the opposite direction and try to optimize your metabolism. And it's a good approach to do after a diet, because it's good to have a healthy metabolism, because that'll help set you up for long-term success in, and weight loss. If you want to do that again, or weight maintenance on higher calories, it's just a good approach overall to keep a healthy metabolism. === FILE: Stop Blaming Your Metabolism [ZDIznY05OLk].txt ===

 biggest weight loss myth holding you back is that your metabolism is slow. Now, I know people don't like hearing this because it feels like an attack, but if you look at the research literature, on average, slow metabolisms do not even come close to explaining the obesity epidemic. In fact, if you look at some pretty clear research data, over 90% of the variance in metabolic rate can be explained by differences in lean mass. Yes, you may have a low energy expenditure, but it's much more likely from a lack of physical activity than it is from a slow metabolism. Even people with severe hypothyroidism have a reduction maximum in resting metabolic rate of about 25%, which could account to several hundred calories. But again, this is untreated hypothyroidism, and these are the largest reductions in metabolic rate we see across the board, and this is in untreated hypothyroidism. So if you don't have untreated hypothyroidism, it's very unlikely that you have a slow metabolism. Why people think they have slow metabolisms is people tend to not be accurate estimators of their food intake. In the same study that demonstrated that over 90% of the variance in people's metabolic rates is due to lean mass, they also showed that on average, people who are overweight or obese under-report their food intake by over 50%, and they over-report their physical activity by about 50%. That is a massive, massive, massive difference. Now, a lot of people will hear that and say, well, you know, that means people are lying about their food intake. No, people are just really poor estimators of their food intake. They forget their snacks, their licks, their bites. They don't realize that things like alcohol, even if you're not having beer or wine, alcohol itself has calories. They forget about that. They forget about small little things they have during the day, and then also they just don't know portion sizes. If you wanna be depressed, go way out of serving a peanut butter. Go way out of serving a ice cream. Go way out of serving a cereal. I promise you, you'll be depressed. So people will track these things kind of loosely and say, well, I'm eating 1,500 calories a day and can't lose weight when in reality they're eating over 2,000 calories per day and can't lose weight. Can individuals have slow metabolisms? They can, but it's not common. And even people who are type 2 diabetic and obese, it's been shown on average, they do not have slower metabolisms than people who are lean or normal weight. And in fact, if anything, they have a slightly faster metabolism and slightly greater total energy expenditure, possibly even when you standardize for lean mass. This idea that people get overweight because of slow metabolisms, is it just not supported by the data? And possibly the strongest research data is that of the GLP-1 memetics out there, like Ozympic, like Wegovie, like Trezeppitide. Those drugs do not increase energy expenditure. What they do is they're a very powerful appetite suppressants so people eat less. And they are the most effective obesity treatments we have. I think the biggest thing I would say is if you're having trouble losing weight, this mindset of, oh, I can't lose weight because my metabolism's slow, it could be a self-limiting belief. And if you aren't tracking things accurately or really paying attention and being diligent, at least for a period of time, to understand truly what food portion sizes are, then this could be holding you back. If you need help with tracking and your nutrition, you definitely want to check out my app, Carbon Diet Coach. It takes care of all the guesswork around how much protein, carbs, fats, how many calories you should eat for your goal. And it makes tracking a breeze. With the barcode scanner, with the food label scanner, it's just so easy to track everything you eat in a day and get a really good idea of what you're actually taking in. So make sure you follow them at Carbon Diet Coach and download and subscribe today.

=== FILE: The Science of Obesity [CkCIg_8lWhQ].txt ===

 s know what? Some people are hardworking and some people are lazy and people who are lazy eat too much and don't move. So while obesity at a mechanistic level is the difference between the energy you consume versus the energy you expend on a long-term basis, w A lot of people have focused on the hormonal side of things and the metabolism side of things, because it does seem intuitive that if some people gain body fat, gain weight, perhaps they have slower metabolisms. Perhaps there are certain hormones that are out of whack that are causing them to be like that. But honestly, the research on this has been very, very underwhelming. People who are obese do not have slower metabolisms on average than people who are lean. In fact, if anything, they have a little bit faster metabolism. And this goes for people who are obese, not type 2 diabetic, or obese and type 2 diabetic. And when you standardize for lean mass between lean and obese people, you basically have the same metabolic rate. If anything, obese people have a little bit faster metabolic rate. So it's not a metabolism issue. Now, if somebody has some sort of genetic defect that causes them to have a slow metabolism, because those things do happen, then yes, that would make them prone for obesity. But on an average, on a population level, slow metabolism does not explain the obesity crisis, because on average, people who are obese do not have slow metabolisms. And on the hormonal side, when we discovered the hormone leptin, we thought that this was going to be the fix-all for everything. And then we found that leptin, insulin, most of these hormones are passive players in obesity. They respond to changes in metabolism due to excessive body fat, not the other way around. So if you are obese, or you gain too much body fat, what happens is your adipocytes, your fat cells, can only store a certain amount of fat in them. In fact, I think it's something like most fat cells kind of max out at like 100 microns of diameter. And so once you get to that size, now you don't really have a place to put the fat, the glucose. And so now you start becoming insulin resistant, because this is now spilling over into the bloodstream. And that's why you see elevated levels of glucose, elevated levels of insulin, elevated levels of blood lipids in type two diabetes, because the fat tissue has kind of been maxed out. Now you can, you can create more fat cells. We believe this does happen that once you go past a certain point, you start creating more fat cells, but you've basically like backed up the train so far that now the lipids, the glucose, they can't get into the cells. And so it starts accumulating in the bloodstream. And that's why you see these elevated levels of blood glucose, blood lipids, HbA1c. And in an effort to fight that, your pancreas, because your blood glucose is elevated, keeps pumping out more insulin. Now, some people have kind of gone with the carbohydrate insulin of obesity, which is the reverse, which is okay, you eat refined carbohydrate, that increases insulin, drives fat into fat cells, traps it there, and you can't access it. That model has been roundly debunked with human randomized control trials. And honestly, like the biggest nail in the coffin really is the GLP-1 memetics, because GLP-1 memetics are the most effective weight loss tools we've ever come across. People on average lose 15 to 20% of their body weight, and they increase insulin, at least acutely. Now, as somebody loses weight and loses body fat, their levels of insulin will go down because they're becoming more insulin sensitive. But in the short term, it increases insulin, which is in direct opposition to what the carbohydrate insulin model of obesity says. These hormones do change, but they are changing in response to the excessive amounts of fat tissue and the metabolic milieu that starts to accumulate in the bloodstream. And then once you have blood lipids, blood glucose, elevated levels of insulin in the bloodstream, that starts a whole cascade of problems where everything is interfering with everything else and making things way worse. So those hormones tend to be passive players. They're not driving the effects. That said, things like thyroid hormone, if you have low levels of thyroid hormone, that can have a direct effect because thyroid hormone does have an impact on your metabolic rate. That sounds like a lot, but let's say somebody has a BMR of like 1600 calories per day. Now, BMR is not the same thing as the total amount of calories you burn per day. That's just your basal metabolic rate. If somebody has a BMR of 1600, for example, calories per day, their total daily energy expenditure, if they're even modestly active, is probably somewhere around 23, 24, 2500 calories a day. You can do high carb. We have that setting or low fat. We also have balanced. We have plant-based. We have ketogenic. Any number of things. And even within those things, you can shimmy the macros to be more towards what you personally prefer. And that is going to help with sustainability of the diet because you can select the diet that feels the least restrictive for you. Number four, events and vacations. This is something not talked about enough, but so many people fall off the wagon on vacation or during events and either slows their progress, stops their progress, or they go backwards. === FILE: Weight Loss Gets Harder Over Time？ [9Y9n91B5ey8].en.txt ===

Why does losing weight get harder over time? Hi, I'm Lane Norton, co-founder of Carbon Diet Coach and PhD in nutritional sciences. And I've coached over 2,000 people during the course of my career one-on-one and have practical in the trenches experience with this as well as understanding the scientific literature. So, anyone who's done a weight loss diet for any period of time knows that whatever calories you start out with, you typically don't just lose weight linearly until the end of time, until you're a emaciated corpse, weight loss slows down and typically eventually stalls, even when you start out in what's a calorie deficit. And this causes a lot of people to be confused and say things like, "Well, I ate in a calorie deficit and it didn't work for me." No, you ate in what was a calorie deficit or what should have been a calorie deficit, but if you didn't lose weight, it wasn't a calorie deficit. Now, how can this happen? Well, we have two sides to an equation, which is energy in, calories in, versus total daily energy expenditure, calories out. And if you consume less calories than you expend, you'll lose weight. But a lot of people have the impression that this is a very static equation. And the reality is both sides of this equation move. As you reduce your calorie intake and begin to lose weight, several things start to happen. The first is you can have a decrease in your basil metabolic rate. Now, your basil metabolic rate is basically the cost of keeping the lights on. So, if I just had you lay down and just breathe, your basil metabolic rate is what you burn over a 24-hour period doing no activity. And so for most people this is actually about 50 to 70% of their total daily energy expenditure or total calories out. Then you have what's called your physical activity. And this encompasses two buckets. Your NEAT non-ex exercise activity thermogenesis and your exercise activity which is what it sounds like how much exercise you do. neat is non-purposeful movements like fidgeting, postural energy, uh, and can actually contribute to a significant amount of your energy expenditure per day. And this is also modifiable during a weight loss diet. So, how much? Well, we know that 10% weight loss can cause approximately a 15% reduction on average in your basil metabolic rate. We also know a 10% reduction in body weight can cause a 400 calorie reduction in your neat non-ex exercise activity thermogenesis. So let's use an example. Let's take myself for instance. I maintain my current body weight about 205 lbs on approximately 3,400 calories per day. If I go down to 2,700 calories per day, that's about a 700 calorie deficit for me. That's a pretty decentsized deficit. But over time, I will lose weight. And let's say I lose 10% of my body weight over time. If my BMR gets reduced by 15%, my BMR is around 2,000 calories per day. That's a 300 calorie reduction per day. And if my meat goes down by 400 calories a day, 300 plus 400 is 700 calories. So if you take 3,400, my original maintenance calories, and you subtract 700, you get 2,700, which was my original calorie deficit. So what started as a calorie deficit, if I lose 10% of my body weight actually ends up my new maintenance calories. Now, this isn't something that just happens like instantaneously or there's not like a tipping point where you reach a certain weight. This happens progressively over time. Additionally, weight loss becomes harder the more weight you lose because your appetite signals become more and more sensitive. Meaning you feel hungrier the longer you diet, the more weight you lose. When you consider that atyposites or your fat cells are like sponges and so essentially they in expand or shrink in size depending on how much fat is being pushed into them or pushed out of them. So in the case of a calorie deficit, you're pushing fat out because you have to create energy to fill that calorie deficit. In the case of a calorie surplus, you're pushing energy into the fat cells to store it. So when fat cells shrink, they actually send out signals telling your brain to be hungrier. When they expand, they send out signals telling you to be less hungry, but there tends to be more regulation on the lower end of things, meaning you can kind of eat past those satiety signals if your fat cells are expanding, but when they're shrinking, that effect becomes very pronounced. It makes sense if you think about from a survival perspective 10,000 years ago, the risk of starvation was much greater than the risk of predation, meaning the appetite regulating signals that would prevent you from becoming too fat would be because it'd be easier for you to get eaten by something because you can't run away as well. And sure, that's a risk, but it's a much lower risk over the course of humanity's existence than starving to death, which is a very, very real risk up until, say, I don't know, the last hundred years or so. And so this has been ingrained into our genetics, our DNA, and it makes it so that the more weight you lose, the more difficult it is to lose more weight after that. Because calorie restriction is kind of sensed like controlled starvation. While it's not starvation, your body, your endocrine system, and your brain are going to respond by trying to drive you back to your previous body weight because that is safer. So those are some of the ways in which your body fights losing more weight. So how do we combat this? Choosing very filling foods, high fiber, high satiety foods, minimally processed. And by understanding that your energy expenditure can change over time. A lot of coaches don't understand this. A lot of apps don't understand this. But Carbon Diet Coach understands this. And by tracking your energy expenditure, and it does that through looking at how your weight changes versus how many calories you're taking in. And based on our custom algorithm, can determine with really good accuracy what your maintenance calories or total daily energy expenditure is. Carbon can make adjustments to get in front of these decreases in total daily energy expenditure. So you don't have to worry about it. It's going to adjust your nutrition automatically for you. So, if you're interested in Carbon Diet Coach, you can follow them here on Instagram.

And while this may seem like a very straightforward question, the answer is pretty complicated, if you want to dig into the details, but in general is actually quite simple. So what I mean by that is if we look at the body of research on various different diets, if we look at them in terms of long-term weight loss, so more than a year, there was a meta-analysis of like 14 different popular diets that was done a few years back, and they looked at all these different popular diets and their effects on long-term weight loss, and what they basically found was there was no difference between these diets. They were all kind of equally bad at facilitating long-term weight loss. Part of that is because people do a diet rather than trying to make a new lifestyle, which is so critically important. We know from successful weight loss maintainers and studies of their habits and behaviors that one of the biggest factors for long-term success is literally changing your life, creating a new lifestyle, habit, behaviors. That is the most important aspect of this, and that is all done to facilitate adherence. Because we know from these studies, even though none of these diets are better than others long-term for weight loss, when they stratify participants based on their level of adherence, what they find is regardless of diet type, there is a linear effect of adherence on weight loss, meaning the more adherent you are, the more weight you lose. The best diet for you is the diet that you can best adhere to, and that may look different for different people. For me, I do flexible dieting, and I like kind of a balanced diet. I like to be able to pick foods from different food groups. If I'm having a fattier meal, I like to be able to accommodate it. If I'm having a higher carb meal, I like to be able to accommodate it, or the mix of both, obviously. Some people, they like low carb way better. They say, I don't feel hungry. It feels easy for me. Some people like time-restricted eating. They say, you know, I'm not hungry during my fasting periods, and then during my feeding period, I feel really satisfied. It still keeps me in a calorie deficit. Again, great tools to facilitate weight loss. Behavior change is very hard to facilitate, no matter what we're talking about. Because it is so difficult, and if you want to lose weight, you have to implement some form of restriction, no matter what you do. Whether it be a dietary restriction, like low carbohydrate or low fat, whether it be a time restriction, like time-restricted eating, or whether it be a tracking restriction, like flexible dieting and tracking your macros, there has to be some form of restriction. But you can choose the form of restriction that feels the least restrictive for you as an individual, and understand that it doesn't necessarily apply to others. That is where the individual variability in diet really seems to be, which is, what trips that compliance algorithm in people's heads where they feel like a diet is something they can make into a lifestyle. They feel like this is something they can do in perpetuity. Because of the diet you're on, if you can't see yourself doing it in six months, 12 months, 18 months, five years, the research shows you're going to put that weight back on, because you're not going to be able to facilitate a long-term lifestyle change. And that is why carbon does not pigeonhole you into any one style of diet. We don't tell you how many meals you've got to eat per day. We don't tell you, hey, you've got to do a balanced diet, or a Mediterranean, or you've got to do low carb, or you've got to do low fat. We give you options that span the gamut. Plus the ability to go in within individual options and still shimmy the macros a little bit towards what you personally prefer while still getting all the results. And if you want to eat seven meals a day, you can eat seven meals a day. If you want to eat two meals a day, you can eat two meals a day. Carbon allows for that flexibility. They also allow for the flexibility to change your calories day to day so that you can facilitate higher calorie days on days when you want more flexibility, lower calorie days, perhaps on days when you have more control over everything. Or if you have an oopsie, you can put it into the diet planner and it will adjust your remaining days automatically without you having to do the math yourself. So carbon is built around the idea of maximizing adherence. Because maximal adherence is going to produce maximal fat loss and the ability for you to keep it off. So again, it's not the sexy answer a lot of people want, but the best diet is the one that you can adhere to. And that is why carbon gives you maximum flexibility for your dietary preference.
